headline: Bay fans buy $300 authentics in San Francisco and $35 tees in the East Bay.
summary: Spending power runs very high at the top of the Bay Area and very uneven across it. Cold, foggy Chase Center nights make layering as big a category as jerseys. Demand follows Curry and Oakland-era nostalgia, so retro outsells the new. After a 37-45 season and a play-in exit, this year sells the Curry era, Specter and the Christmas game, not a title chase.

insights.title: Curry demand, with an aging core on the clock
insights.detail: Curry is still the dominant jersey and tee driver. The 2026-27 story is an aging core running it back after missing out on a star, with Butler and Moody recovering from injury. Fans buy Curry as a legacy purchase, partly from urgency: his career is in its final chapters.
insights.implication: Build Curry-anchored 'while it lasts' product and commemorative capsules. Hold back on secondary names such as rookie Yaxel Lendeborg until they stick.

insights.title: Two economies, two price tiers
insights.detail: San Francisco, the Peninsula and Silicon Valley skew very high income, with big stock-compensation and bonus cycles. Oakland, the East Bay and parts of the South Bay are far more price-conscious. So the same fan might buy a $300 authentic or a $35 tee, depending on where they live. Chase Center is in San Francisco, but the team's 47-year Oakland history keeps a large East Bay fan base that still identifies with the Oakland era.
insights.implication: Tier the assortment. Offer premium authentic and limited collab pieces to SF and Silicon Valley buyers, and accessible swingman, tee and kids product to the East Bay. Put Oakland-era heritage graphics in both.

insights.title: Cold, foggy nights make layering the core category
insights.detail: Bay summers are cool and foggy, and the bayfront arena district turns cold after dark. Hoodies, crewnecks, track jackets, beanies and shells sell much of the year. Shorts get a short window from September to October. Warm-ups and shells are bought for the commute and the game, not only the fan moment.
insights.implication: Weight the assortment toward hooded and quarter-zip warm-ups, packable shells and heavy tees. Treat shorts and light mesh as a narrow early-fall and playoff-run story.

insights.title: Retro and Oakland-era nostalgia outsells the new
insights.detail: We Believe yellow, the 1960s 'The City' script, the 'Oakland' tribute lineage, and Run TMC and Splash-era looks have a durable resale and thrift market. They turn up at Bay flea markets and vintage dealers. Many fans buy older looks first and the current jersey second.
insights.implication: Build heritage capsules and reissues around the Oakland-era marks, with clear licensing through the team and NBA. Price them as collector pieces.

insights.title: Marquee games drive gifting and drops
insights.detail: The Oct 21 ESPN game at the Lakers, the Dec 25 Denver nightcap at Chase Center and the NBA Cup group stage are natural drop moments. Christmas is the single biggest gifting date. Specter uniforms and their merchandise collection launched Sept 9, so holiday demand will test them against the Association, Icon, Statement and City jerseys.
insights.implication: Run the Specter and City Edition holiday push from early November through mid-December. Add Christmas-Day-specific product and a December 25 tie-in at Chase Center.

insights.title: Resale and vintage are a main channel
insights.detail: The Bay has a deep vintage, thrift and resale scene, from Haight Street and Mission shops to monthly flea markets such as the Alameda Point Antiques Faire. Fans expect to find older Warriors product there. Online resale competes directly with new retail for the same buyer.
insights.implication: Use limited runs, numbering and story-driven drops so new product isn't measured against cheap vintage. Consider authenticated reissues that resale buyers will trust.

insights.title: High sales tax, no tax holiday
insights.detail: California has no sales-tax holiday, and combined rates in Bay cities run high: roughly 8.6 percent in San Francisco and over 10 percent in Oakland. Shoppers don't wait for a tax-free window. They respond to brand promotions and free shipping.
insights.implication: Offer free-shipping thresholds, member early access and gift-with-purchase. Skip discounts timed to a tax holiday.

places.name: Chase Center and Thrive City
places.why: Home arena and team store, plus the game-night flow where cold-weather layering and Specter and City jersey sales concentrate.

places.name: Union Square
places.why: The main tourist and holiday retail district, with heavy Christmas window and gifting traffic and out-of-town visitors buying Warriors gear.

places.name: Stonestown Galleria
places.why: A neighborhood mall for the city's western and southern residents, who skew toward everyday, value-minded sneaker and apparel shopping.

places.name: Westfield Valley Fair and Santana Row
places.why: The Silicon Valley premium-retail anchor, where high household incomes and tech-worker gifting favor authentic and limited product.

places.name: Oakland Coliseum
places.why: The Warriors' Oakland home until 2019. Oakland-era graphics and We Believe nostalgia still land in the East Bay.

places.name: Alameda Point Antiques Faire
places.why: A long-running monthly vintage market where retro Warriors and Oakland sports apparel changes hands.

places.name: Haight Street and the Mission District
places.why: The city's vintage, thrift and streetwear shops, where retro sports apparel and sneaker resale culture live.

people.name: Stephen Curry
people.why: The main driver of jersey, tee and sneaker demand in the market, with a legacy-purchase effect as his career matures.

people.name: Draymond Green
people.why: The second most recognizable Warriors voice, and a steady seller of attitude-driven tees and fan product.

people.name: Steve Kerr
people.why: The face of 'Strength in Numbers', and a reference point for fans who buy the team's culture, not only its stars.

people.name: Joe Lacob
people.why: His ownership built Chase Center and Thrive City and shapes the premium, San Francisco-centered retail strategy.

people.name: Marshawn Lynch
people.role: Oakland-born former NFL running back and entrepreneur
people.why: His Oakland-rooted Beast Mode brand shows how local pride apparel sells in the East Bay. It is a model for Oakland collaboration done right.

people.name: Damian Lillard
people.why: A prominent Oakland native. East Bay audiences follow him beyond the Warriors, and his hometown pride is a reference point for them.

moments.name: NBA opening week and Cup Nights
moments.why: The season-opening window (Warriors at the Lakers on Oct 21) and Cup group nights bring the first sustained demand spike of the year.

moments.name: Black Friday and the holiday shopping run
moments.why: The biggest gifting and promotional stretch, with Union Square, Valley Fair and online all peaking.

moments.name: Christmas Day at Chase Center (Denver)
moments.why: The 10:30 p.m. ET nightcap is a marquee home date and a natural anchor for gift and special-edition product.

moments.name: Lunar New Year
moments.why: A major gifting and red-and-gold apparel moment, in a Bay Area with some of the country's largest Chinese American communities.

moments.name: NBA All-Star Weekend
moments.why: A national fashion and drop moment. Curry-era star demand often spikes around it.

moments.name: Playoff push and Play-In
moments.why: If the team contends, playoff gear and shells surge fast. Last year's play-in exit shows how quickly demand can switch off.

moments.name: Back to school
moments.why: Bay Area school years start in mid-August, pulling sneaker, backpack and kids' apparel spending into July and early August.

moments.name: Fleet Week and fall events
moments.why: San Francisco's fall tourism peak brings visitors, and out-of-town purchases around the opener.

productHooks: A cold-night 'Chase Center' kit: heavyweight hooded warm-up, packable shell and fog-gray beanie, sold as a bundle at Thrive City and online.
An Oakland-era heritage capsule (licensed wordmarks, We Believe yellow tee, retro warm-up), priced at accessible and premium tiers for the East Bay and collectors.
Christmas Day 2026 Denver game capsule: a numbered tee and hoodie drop timed for Dec 25 and the holiday gift window.

A premium authentic and limited Specter-collection offer for Silicon Valley and San Francisco buyers, with early access for members. Lead with team marks, and add Curry-named product only once his licensing is confirmed.
Lunar New Year red-and-gold Warriors capsule for the early-February window, developed with Bay Area Asian American designers who are credited and paid.
watchouts: Oakland-era marks and the Oakland relocation still stir strong feelings in the East Bay. Credit Oakland, partner with Oakland-based creators and don't treat Oakland as a nostalgia prop.
Co-create Lunar New Year and other cultural gifting product with local Asian American designers, and credit them. Avoid generic red-and-gold dragon clichés.
Old team marks, wordmarks and the We Believe name are third-party IP owned by the team and NBA. Get licensing before any reissue.
Demand rides on Curry and an aging core with injury questions. Don't over-forecast depth players or assume contention.

extra.priceProfile: Highly split. San Francisco, the Peninsula and Silicon Valley have very high household incomes and stock-compensation cycles that support authentic and premium pricing. Oakland, the East Bay and parts of the South Bay are markedly more price-conscious. California has no sales-tax holiday and a statewide base rate of 7.25 percent. Combined rates run roughly 8.6 percent in San Francisco, about 10 percent in Oakland and 9 percent or more in San Jose. Tier the line: premium authentic and limited drops at one end, accessible swingman, tee and kids product at the other.
extra.jerseyBehavior: Fans buy Curry first, then other current players. A notable share buys retro and Oakland-era jerseys and tees through vintage and resale channels. Authentic jerseys sell mainly to premium buyers in San Francisco and Silicon Valley. Swingman and tees dominate game-night and East Bay purchases. Kids' and youth sizes spike around Christmas and back-to-school. Knockoffs and unlicensed shirts circulate at flea markets and online.
